method: Rebuild from primary text. The clause previously cited 'IWC Wage Order (industry-specific)' — a body of law with no provision in it, which is why it was one of the twelve clauses the validator flagged as unverifiable as filed. IWC Order No. 4-2001 §12 was fetched as a PDF from the Department of Industrial Relations, the body that publishes the wage orders, and read verbatim; Cal. Lab. Code §226.7 was fetched from the California Legislative Counsel and both enacted versions were read. The body was rewritten from those texts and checked against the construing case law on CourtListener. Assertions describe the REBUILT body.
queries: Brinker rest period ten minutes major fraction thereof
Augustus ABM Security Services rest period relinquish control on call

assertions.text: the employer shall authorize and permit rest periods, which insofar as practicable shall be in the middle of each work period
assertions.note: Wage Order 4 §12(A), verbatim. 'Authorize and permit' is the operative verb and it is weaker than 'provide'; the previous body used 'authorized and permitted' correctly.

assertions.text: rest time is ten minutes net per four hours or major fraction thereof, which yields 10 minutes for 3½–6 hours, 20 for more than 6 up to 10, and 30 for more than 10 up to 14
assertions.note: The rate is Wage Order 4 §12(A) verbatim. The schedule is Brinker's construction of those same words, quoted below. This is the correction that matters: the Court of Appeal had read the identical language to give a seven-hour shift only 10 minutes, and the Supreme Court reversed. The previous body reproduced the raw words and left the reader free to reach the rejected answer.

assertions.text: no rest period need be authorized where total daily work time is less than three and one-half hours
assertions.note: Wage Order 4 §12(A), third sentence, verbatim. Absent from the previous body, which stated the entitlement without its floor.

assertions.text: rest periods are counted as hours worked with no deduction from wages
assertions.note: Wage Order 4 §12(A), final sentence; and §226.7(d), which adds that the subdivision 'is declaratory of existing law'.

assertions.text: a rest period must be off duty: the employer must relieve the employee of all duties and relinquish control, and may not require the employee to remain on call
assertions.note: Augustus v. ABM Security Services, quoted below. This is the construction the previous body had no trace of, and it is the one that decides most rest-period disputes in practice — an employer that lets people take the break at their desk with a radio on has not provided it.

assertions.text: the premium is one additional hour of pay for each workday a rest period is not provided, at the regular rate of compensation, which includes non-discretionary payments
assertions.note: Wage Order 4 §12(B) and §226.7(c) for the premium; Ferra for the measure. The previous body did not state the premium at all — it described the entitlement and stopped — even though the clause's own rationale asserts 'The premium is the same one hour per day.'

assertions.text: the off-duty rule has been displaced for a registered security officer employed by a registered private patrol operator under a qualifying collective bargaining agreement
assertions.note: §226.7(f), added by Stats. 2020, Ch. 343. §226.7(f)(5) says so in terms: 'it is the intent of the Legislature to abrogate, for the security services industry only, the California Supreme Court's decision in Augustus v. ABM Security Services, Inc. (2016) 2 Cal.5th 257, to the extent that decision is in conflict with this subdivision.' The conditions in §226.7(f)(3) are cumulative and narrow, and §226.7(f)(4) excludes cases filed before January 1, 2021. Note that this subdivision is in the version of §226.7 that is repealed on January 1, 2027; the later operative version added by Stats. 2020, Ch. 343, Sec. 3 does not contain it.

priorDefects: citation-gap: the only citation was 'IWC Wage Order (industry-specific)', which names a body of law and no provision. Nothing in the clause could be looked up.
omitted: the rest-period schedule Brinker derived from the same words. A reader applying '10 minutes per four hours or major fraction' unaided can land on the reading the Supreme Court reversed.
omitted: the premium entirely, though the clause's rationale asserts it.
omitted: that rest periods must be off duty and cannot be on call (Augustus).
omitted: that rest time counts as hours worked with no deduction.

unsupported: 'Rest periods may not be combined with meal periods or waived in exchange for leaving early.' No provision of Wage Order 4 or the Labor Code read here says this. It is carried into the rebuilt body with an explicit NOT VERIFIED marker rather than dropped or asserted.
gaps: Order No. 4-2001 is the order read; the clause fires for every California employer and the other sixteen orders were not read. Order 16 (construction, drilling, logging and mining) in particular has its own rest-period provision.

The no-combining / no-early-departure rule is carried unverified. It is standard employer practice and it is a fair inference from 'insofar as practicable shall be in the middle of each work period', but it is an inference, and the DLSE guidance that states it is the agency's reading rather than the text.
Whether the ten minutes runs from when the employee reaches a break area, and whether travel to it is on the employer's time, was not researched. Augustus decides control, not measurement.

§226.7(e) exempts employees who are exempt from meal or rest requirements under other state law. The rebuilt clause is addressed to non-exempt employees and does not state the exemption boundary; a reader classifying a borderline employee gets no help from it.

judicialQuotations.case: Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (Cal. 2012) 53 Cal.4th 1004
judicialQuotations.quote: The combined effect of the two pertinent sentences, giving full effect to each, is this; Employees are entitled to 10 minutes' rest for shifts from three and one-half to six hours in length, 20 minutes for shifts of more than six hours up to 10 hours, 30 minutes for shifts of more than 10 hours up to 14 hours, and so on.

judicialQuotations.case: Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (Cal. 2012) 53 Cal.4th 1004 — describing and rejecting the Court of Appeal's reading
judicialQuotations.quote: In its view, employees are entitled to 10 minutes' rest for shifts of three and one-half hours or more, to 20 minutes' rest for shifts of seven and one-half hours or more, and so on. An employee working a seven-hour shift thus would be entitled to only 10 minutes' rest.

judicialQuotations.case: Augustus v. ABM Security Services, Inc. (Cal. 2016) 2 Cal.5th 257
judicialQuotations.quote: What we conclude is that state law prohibits on-duty and on-call rest periods. During required rest periods, employers must relieve their employees of all duties and relinquish any control over how employees spend their break time.

abrogationNote: Augustus was partly abrogated by statute, but only for one industry: §226.7(f)(5) says the Legislature intended to abrogate it 'for the security services industry only'. Anyone reading this finding should not generalise from that subdivision. It also sits in the version of §226.7 that repeals itself on January 1, 2027; the successor version enacted in the same chapter has no subdivision (f).
